description_full: VTEX, together with its subsidiaries, provides software-as-a-service digital commerce platform for enterprise brands and retailers. It provides VTEX platform that enables customers to execute commerce strategy, including building online stores, and integrating and managing orders across channels, as well as creating marketplaces to sell products from third-party vendors. The company also offers customer support services; and optional services, such as project management, solutions architecting, and implementation consulting services. It serves its products to home appliances, apparel and accessories, beauty and health, electronics, grocery, department stores, and toys and hobbies, as well as home, furniture, and decoration markets. The company has operations in Brazil, Argentina, Chile, Colombia, France, Italy, Mexico, Peru, Portugal, Romania, Spain, the United Kingdom, the United States, and internationally. VTEX was founded in 2000 and is headquartered in Grand Cayman, Cayman Islands.
ceo_bio: Mr. Geraldo  do Carmo Thomaz Jr. | Co-founder, Co-CEO, Co-Chairman & Chief Technology Officer | Age 47
culture_narrative: Employs approximately 1K people. Revenue per employee of $211K ranks in the bottom quartile among Technology peers. Each employee generates $28K of free cash flow annually. Stock-based compensation of $15K per employee reflects an ownership culture.
financial_summary: VTEX is a small-cap technology business with a $525M market cap on $241M of annual revenue.
Returns on capital run at 39% against a 11% cost of capital — a 28-point spread that is the clearest signature of an economic moat. Gross margins of 77% confirm genuine pricing power.

The business throws off $32M in free cash flow — roughly 13 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders, and cash conversion sits at 1.67× so those profits are backed by real cash.
On the balance sheet, the balance sheet carries net cash, which is the gold standard: the business never has to make desperate decisions in a bad year, and interest coverage of 40× is fortress-like.

Management returns a meaningful 11.3% of market cap to owners through dividends and buybacks, a strong signal of disciplined capital allocation, and insiders hold 48% of the shares, so management thinks like owners because it is one — the strongest alignment there is, and profit capture is only 0.3× the fair share, suggesting no structural edge inside its industry.

sect: Its 8% operating margin is roughly in line with the Technology median (7%).

The sector is fragmented and competitive (HHI 0.03 across 535 companies in the universe; the top four hold 29% of revenue), so pricing power is hard to come by.
mkt: The shares have drifted higher, up 11% over the past year excluding the latest month, though it has pulled back 12% over the last three months.
The price sits mid-way through its 52-week range, 30% below the high.
With annualised volatility of 44% and a beta of 1.13, it moves roughly with the market, though its beta has shifted (1y 0.56 vs 5y 1.23), so read it loosely.
About $2.5M trades a day, enough to build a position.
In past sell-offs it fell 74% in the 2022 bear market.
val: The price sits above its DCF fair value of $2.90 (margin of safety -11%), so there is no valuation cushion.
The fair-value models disagree (dispersion 40%), and the Monte Carlo range runs $2.54 to $3.41 (P10-P90), so treat the estimate as noisy.
On multiples it looks cheap against Technology peers: EV/EBITDA 9.5 vs 16.1 and P/FCF 16.2 vs 23.3 (sector median).
Earnings yields are mixed: an FCF yield of 6.2% (above the risk-free rate) and an EBIT/EV of 5.2% (vs the 8% bar).
The 10 covering analysts target $5.51 on average, 71% above the price, well away from the model's fair value.
The price implies 9.9% annual cash-flow growth, 3pp more than the model expects.
prof: ROIC of 39% clears the cost of capital of 10.9% by 28pp, the mark of a value creator.
It runs a 77% gross margin and converts 13% of revenue into free cash flow, or 6% after stock compensation.
Earnings quality is mixed: cash conversion of 1.67x, but a weak Piotroski score of 3/9.
ROE of 9% comes mostly from margins and asset turnover rather than leverage (1.5x equity multiplier).
It spends 26.6% of revenue on R&D and 7.2% on stock compensation (above the 2% gate).
hlth: The balance sheet carries net cash of $181.9M (37% of market cap).
growth: At current returns, reinvesting 100% of profits supports about 30.0% a year of fundamental growth, enough to sustain growth.
Capex runs only 0.3x depreciation (0.4% of sales), so the asset base is being harvested rather than grown.
It has beaten earnings estimates by 49.8% on average.
Analysts expect 17.3% long-term annual earnings growth.
own: Insiders own 47.7%, meaningful skin in the game, and institutions hold 35%.
Insiders have only sold over the past year (15 sales, net $2.0M sold).
It returns 11.3% a year to shareholders (11.3% in buybacks).
people: With about 1,139 employees, each generates about $211K of revenue, 0.6x the Technology median.
That works out to $28K of free cash flow per employee.
The company is founder-led, which often keeps management aligned with long-term owners.
